analysis.one_liner: Extends the limit on airline liability for damages from terrorist attacks through 2003.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee and died there at the end of the 107th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: After the September 11 attacks, Congress capped at $100 million the amount airlines had to pay for damages to third parties (such as people on the ground and businesses near Ground Zero) caused by terrorist attacks, and this bill would have extended that cap from its original expiration in early 2002 through December 31, 2003. If a hijacked plane caused massive casualties or property damage, taxpayers and victims—not the airline—would bear costs above $100 million. The bill was introduced in March 2002 and sent to committee, where it remained until the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the airlines would have gained certainty and financial protection: no matter how enormous the third-party losses from a terrorist attack on their planes, their liability would have been capped at $100 million in aggregate, shifting the rest of the potential burden to victims and, indirectly, to taxpayers (a related law, the Air Transportation Safety and System Stabilization Act, channeled victim compensation through a federal fund).

how_it_helps.text: Caps air carrier liability for third-party damages from any single act of terrorism at $100 million in aggregate for all claims, versus uncapped liability otherwise.
Extends the protection period from the original post-9/11 window through December 31, 2003, covering flights for nearly two additional years.
Includes a technical correction to a cross-reference in the Aviation and Transportation Security Act, effective November 19, 2001.

analysis.who_pays: People and businesses harmed by a future terrorist attack on an aircraft: any claims beyond $100 million in aggregate would go unpaid by the airline, leaving victims without full compensation. (The separate federal victim compensation fund, created by the same 2001 law, absorbed much of the ground-victim compensation cost, which was ultimately paid largely by taxpayers.)

drawbacks.text: Caps aggregate liability at $100 million regardless of how many people are harmed; a catastrophic attack could generate claims in the billions, most of which victims could not recover from the airline.

The bill's core protection runs through December 31, 2003, long after the immediate post-9/11 crisis that justified it, raising the objection that the subsidy had become a routine industry protection rather than an emergency measure.
Because liability is capped, airlines have less financial incentive to invest in preventing third-party harm (such as ground casualties), a classic moral-hazard concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cap gave airlines a predictable ceiling on potentially catastrophic, uninsurable losses and may have helped keep the industry flying after 9/11; but it did so by shifting risk onto terrorism victims and taxpayers, and the extension pushed an emergency measure into ordinary times. The bill's death in committee spared victims that shift for the 2002–2003 period.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee from March 2002 until the Congress ended in January 2003, never reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Representative John Mica introduced the bill on March 20, 2002, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee; no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 107th Congress.
The bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, without any vote in committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Potential victims of future aviation terrorism in 2002–2003, who avoided having their recoveries from airlines capped at $100 million per attack. Airlines lost the extended liability protection, though the industry ultimately obtained similar protections through other means (including later terrorism-insurance legislation and risk-sharing arrangements). Short of that, working people bore no new cost because nothing was enacted.

for.name: Rep. John Mica
for.role: House sponsor (R-FL), Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the airline liability cap through 2003.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as committee chair controlled whether the bill ever got a markup or floor vote.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee / Aviation Subcommittee leadership
against.role: Committee and subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after referral, letting it die without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred; the bill was sponsored by a Republican with a single Republican cosponsor, so its support was thin and partisan-shaped, but its fate was committee inaction rather than a recorded split.

industries.note: The bill would have extended their $100 million cap on liability for third-party damages from terrorist attacks; because it died, they remained exposed above that amount during 2002–2003. The industry's interest ran against victims' interest in full compensation.
